title: Landscape shading in pyrography
subtitle: How to build graduated tonal shading for sky, ground, and distance in a pyrography landscape
excerpt: Landscape shading in pyrography creates depth with graduated tone: light in the background, dark in the foreground. This guide walks through a simple tree-and-field composition covering tonal zones and texture rendering.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Book of Drawing and Design (1899) for the tonal gradation and texture shading method in pyrography.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of burning designs into wood using a heated metal tip.
Building up areas of graduated tone by making overlapping passes with the pen tip at consistent speed.
The visual effect where objects appear lighter and less detailed as they recede into the distance, used in landscape composition to create the illusion of depth.

content.text: uses the pen's tonal range to build depth: barely-tan at low heat to near-black at high heat.
is the foundation: the background is the lightest tone; the foreground is the darkest.

When burning any landscape, field scene, or natural view that requires tonal depth rather than simple outline work. The same approach applies to depicting fog, mist, and atmosphere in any landscape subject.

A seasoned lime or birch panel, at least 20 cm × 15 cm, sanded to 240 grit. A pyrography pen with a writing tip (for detail work and horizon lines) and a shading or spoon tip (for area shading). The shading tip covers more area per pass and produces smoother graduated tones than a writing tip.

Plan the landscape in three tonal zones before starting: background (lightest, 20, 30% of maximum burn depth), middle ground (medium, 40, 60%), and foreground (darkest, 70, 90%). Sketch these zones lightly in pencil on the panel. The sky is part of the background zone. The distant treeline or hedgerow is in the middle ground. The nearest field, path, or vegetation is in the foreground.

Start at the background zone. Set the pen to low heat. Work horizontal passes across the background zone, moving the pen at consistent speed. The passes should overlap by about 30%, each pass covers a strip that runs over the previous one slightly. The background should emerge as a barely-visible warm tan. Two to three passes produce the right depth for a distant sky or hazy background.

Increase the pen temperature slightly or slow the pen speed. Work the middle ground with slightly closer-spaced passes, or add a second layer on top of the first pass. The middle ground should be noticeably darker than the background, but the transition between them should be gradual, work the passes so they overlap at the boundary between zones, producing a soft edge rather than a hard line.
The foreground is the darkest zone and the most textured. For a grass field: short irregular marks in the

direction, varying the pen angle slightly between marks, at a medium-slow speed. For tree bark: vertical marks in the tone direction, some short, some longer, overlapping slightly. For a path or track: horizontal passes as in the background but at much lower speed, with occasional darker marks for stones or ruts. All foreground texture should be built up in two layers: a base tone, then detail marks on top.

Switch to the writing tip for horizon lines and any foreground elements that need a defined edge. Tree branches and treeline detail also need the writing tip. The writing tip at medium heat produces a controlled thin line that defines the hard edges in the middle ground and foreground. The background rarely needs any writing-tip detail, its deliberately soft quality is part of the aerial perspective effect.

attrs.symptom: The tonal graduation is not smooth, there are visible lines between the shading passes
attrs.cause: The passes are not overlapping enough, or the pen speed changed between passes
attrs.fix: Increase the overlap between adjacent passes to 50%: each pass should cover half the width of the previous one. Keep the pen moving at exactly the same speed on each pass. If lines are already burned in, add a diagonal pass across all of them at a slightly lower temperature, this blends the row pattern into the overall tone.
